# The Bench at the End of the Route

On his first Monday of retirement, Martin Vale went to inspect a bench.

He had not intended to. He had intended to buy oranges, return a library book about the construction of medieval roofs, and begin whatever people meant when they told him to enjoy himself. But the bench stood outside the old tram depot, and one of its slats had developed a split around a bolt.

Martin stopped.

The split was not yet dangerous. It was, however, becoming dangerous in an organized and determined way.

He set his oranges down.

“Don’t,” said a woman behind him.

Martin turned. She was wearing a yellow raincoat under a cloudless sky and carrying a paper cup of coffee.

“I haven’t done anything.”

“You’ve got the look.”

“What look?”

“The look men get before explaining why a perfectly usable thing has to be taken away.”

Martin straightened. “I was a carpenter for thirty-eight years.”

“Then you ought to know a bench when you see one.”

“I do. That’s how I know this one needs repairing.”

The woman considered him.

“Repairing is permitted,” she said.

She sat at the sound end of the bench and placed her coffee beside her. Martin noticed that she did not test the seat before trusting it. People rarely did. They lowered their whole weight onto the confidence of strangers.

“Are you waiting for a bus?” he asked.

“No.”

“The stop’s been closed for six years.”

“I know. I drove the last bus.”

He looked at the faded sign above them.

“Number eighteen?”

“Seventeen. The eighteen went to the hospital. People confused them constantly. You could tell which passengers had done it by the particular way they looked disappointed.”

Martin picked up his oranges.

“I’ll bring a spanner tomorrow.”

“I’m Vera,” the woman said.

He told her his name.

“Tomorrow, then, Martin. Try not to retire too hard in the meantime.”

***

His wife, June, found the spanner beside the bread bin that evening.

“Already?”

“It’s one bolt.”

“It usually is.”

June had spent thirty-six years married to a man who could turn the purchase of milk into an emergency assessment of shelving. She did not resent it, exactly. Their kitchen drawers ran smoothly. Their doors closed without protest. But she had booked a train journey for Thursday, and she put the tickets under his dinner plate.

“We are going to the sea.”

“I remember.”

“You are not taking anything with a rechargeable battery.”

“The phone?”

“The phone is on probation.”

The following morning, Martin returned to the depot with the spanner, two clamps, a drill, a length of oak, and a small tin of exterior screws.

Vera looked at the bag.

“A complicated bolt.”

“It’s better to have what you need.”

“It must be exhausting to be right so far in advance.”

He knelt beside the bench. It was older than he had first thought. The iron ends had been painted green over black over something reddish that might have been primer or municipal optimism. The wooden slats were oak, weathered silver where hands and rain had worn through the finish.

Under the broken slat, folded into the narrow space between wood and iron, he found a piece of paper.

He almost brushed it away with the grit.

Then he saw the writing.

**If you find this, I got the job.**

Nothing else. No name, no date.

Vera leaned forward.

“Well?”

He handed it to her.

“That’s nice,” she said.

“It might have been put there before the interview.”

“Still nice.”

“It could mean they didn’t get it.”

Vera read the note again.

“You’ve been retired two days and already you’re investigating happiness.”

Martin looked underneath the bench.

There were more papers.

A blue corner showed behind the central support. Something white had been rolled tightly and pushed into a bolt hole that no longer held a bolt. Beneath one iron foot lay a flat stone with an envelope tucked under it.

He sat back on his heels.

“What is this?”

“A bench,” Vera said. “Although I appreciate it’s developing complications.”

They removed the papers carefully.

There were eleven altogether.

Three were too damaged to read. One was a shopping list, unless “milk, batteries, forgive Alan” had some less ordinary purpose. Another contained a telephone number with one digit missing.

The envelope held a letter written in a child’s block capitals.

**Dear Future,**

**Please have dogs.**

Vera laughed so abruptly that coffee escaped through the lid of her cup.

Martin laid the notes on a clean cloth.

He had expected rot. He had brought tools for rot. He had no equipment for this.

***

For the next week, the notes occupied the end of Martin and June’s kitchen table.

They went to the sea on Thursday. Martin took only his phone, and when they passed a public shelter with a gutter hanging loose, June silently took his hand.

They ate chips overlooking a beach empty except for two determined children and a dog carrying something too large for it.

“Perhaps people leave notes everywhere,” June said.

Martin had been telling her about the bench between other subjects.

“Not eleven.”

“Eleven that survived.”

He watched the dog attempting to negotiate a fence with its enormous stick.

“What would you write?”

“To put under a bench?”

“Yes.”

June thought about it.

“Probably something I wouldn’t tell you.”

He turned toward her.

She smiled without apologizing.

“That’s rather the point, isn’t it?”

When they got home, he stopped trying to identify the writers.

Before that, he had searched the telephone number in several possible forms and held the job note against a lamp, hoping for the ghost of a date. Now he put each readable scrap into a clear sleeve.

The following Monday, he took them to the depot.

Vera was there with two coffees.

“I didn’t know how you took it.”

“Milk, no sugar.”

“Good. I guessed that. You look suspicious of sugar.”

They spread the sleeves between them.

There was a note that read, **I’m leaving on Friday. Nobody here knows yet.**

Another said, **You were right about the pear tree.**

A third was simply a drawing of a house with wheels.

Martin’s favorite, though he would not have called it that, had been written on the back of a bus ticket.

**Today I did not go back.**

He had turned that one over many times.

Vera touched its plastic sleeve.

“Could be something terrible.”

“Yes.”

“Could be someone who quit a terrible job.”

“Yes.”

“Could be somebody resisting a second slice of cake.”

Martin looked at her.

“Not everything has to be the biggest thing,” she said.

Traffic moved past the depot. Across the road, a delivery driver was carrying flowers into a building that had once been a bank. The vault was now a room for pottery classes. Martin knew this because he had repaired its door.

“What should we do with them?” he asked.

“What were they doing before?”

“Getting wet.”

“Besides that.”

He considered the question.

“Waiting to be found, perhaps.”

“Perhaps.”

Vera finished her coffee.

“You’ve repaired the bench?”

“Yes.”

“Then I suppose we ought to sit on it.”

So they did.

After a while, they talked about oranges, which had lately become expensive and difficult to peel.

***

The trouble arrived in a white van.

It parked beside the depot on a Wednesday morning, and a young woman in a reflective vest climbed out carrying a tablet. She photographed the pavement, the faded stop sign, the bench, and Martin, who happened to be standing beside it.

“Sorry,” she said. “Could you move?”

“What for?”

“Asset survey.”

He moved six inches.

She lowered the tablet.

“Preferably out of the photograph.”

Her name was Leila, and she worked for the council. The depot frontage was being redesigned. There would be bicycle stands, better drainage, a tree pit, and a new bench.

“What’s wrong with this bench?” Martin asked.

Leila crouched to examine his repair.

“Nothing obvious.”

“Then why replace it?”

“The new seating has backs and armrests. This model’s difficult for some people to get up from.”

Martin looked at the bench again.

It had no back. Its iron ends curled decoratively downward, offering nothing useful to grip.

He had repaired it perfectly without once asking whether it was a good bench.

Vera, who had been listening, planted both feet and stood with a small forward swing.

“She’s right,” she said.

“You never mentioned it.”

“You never asked.”

Leila explained that sound furniture could sometimes be relocated rather than scrapped. There was a community garden behind the library. They had requested somewhere to sit near the raised beds.

“It depends on transport,” she said. “And approval.”

Martin disliked both words. They were the sort of words that made a simple object disappear into six weeks of email.

Nevertheless, he took her address.

At home, he began composing a message.

June read the first paragraph over his shoulder.

“You sound as though you’re declaring war on the bicycle stands.”

“I’m establishing the history.”

“You haven’t reached a verb.”

He deleted most of it.

Then he wrote: **The bench is sound following repair. Could we arrange a site visit at the community garden?**

Leila replied the next morning.

**Yes. Thursday at ten?**

Martin stared at the screen.

“What?” June asked.

“Nothing. Apparently that works.”

The garden committee consisted of four people with incompatible views about compost and complete agreement that they needed a bench.

They chose a spot beneath a plum tree.

Martin checked the ground. Leila checked the access path. A man named Gordon explained, at length, why the plums never ripened properly.

Nobody asked Martin to take charge of anything.

He found this restful for almost seven minutes.

Then he offered to build a firm base.

***

The bench moved in September.

By then, Martin knew that Vera had driven buses for thirty-one years, disliked television quizzes, and could reverse a vehicle into a space that would have made him reconsider the journey.

He also knew why she still visited the depot.

“I liked finishing here,” she told him.

They were waiting for the council truck. The bench stood beside them, freed from the pavement for the first time in decades.

“Last stop, engine off. There’s a little sound a bus makes after you switch it off. Not immediately. A few seconds later.”

“What sort of sound?”

“A settling sound.”

Martin nodded.

“You knew you’d brought it back,” she said. “Whatever happened during the day, that bit was done.”

“And now?”

“Now things don’t finish as clearly.”

He understood that better than he wanted to.

At work, he had complained about deadlines, material deliveries, late changes, people who wanted solid wood at the price of sawdust. Yet each job had eventually become something you could point to.

Retirement had given him days without edges.

The truck arrived. Two workers lifted the bench while Martin tried not to give advice. One worker noticed his expression.

“We move quite a lot of benches,” she assured him.

“Of course.”

“Occasional table, too.”

Vera watched him swallow three separate instructions.

At the garden, the bench was lowered onto its new base beneath the plum tree. Gordon appeared with a spirit level, found that it was level, and looked mildly deprived.

Everyone sat on it in turns.

“It wants a cushion,” said one committee member.

“It wants people with muddy trousers,” said another.

Leila took a photograph.

Martin had brought the notes in a small wooden box he had made from the offcut of the replacement slat. He explained where they had come from.

The committee listened.

“An archive,” Gordon said immediately.

“Perhaps the library could display them,” Leila suggested.

“Some seem private,” Vera said.

They all looked at the box.

Martin had spent several evenings making it. The lid fitted neatly. There was a rubber seal around the edge to keep out damp. He had even tested it under the kitchen tap.

“I thought they might stay with the bench,” he said.

“Underneath?”

“There’s room for a bracket.”

Gordon frowned. “People might add things.”

Nobody spoke.

Then June, who had arrived carrying a bag of apples from their tree, said, “Yes. They might.”

***

The new bench outside the depot had a back, three armrests, and an excellent view of the bicycle stands.

Vera approved.

She still went there sometimes, but not every morning. On Tuesdays she helped a neighbor practice for her driving test. On Fridays she took the eighteen to the hospital, where her sister volunteered in the shop, and they ate lunch together.

Martin went to the community garden when he had a reason.

Sometimes the reason was merely that it was there.

In October, he found a fresh note in the box.

**The plums are better if you get them before Gordon.**

He closed the lid without investigating.

By winter there were seven new notes. One was a recipe. One was a complaint about the recipe. A third, written in green ink, said, **I sat here with my father. He liked the cold.**

Martin made no record of them.

He had briefly considered dates, categories, a notebook documenting additions. Instead, he checked the seal, tightened the bracket, and left people their unmeasured business.

On a bright morning in February, he found Vera sitting beneath the bare plum tree.

She had brought a flask.

“Coffee?”

“Please.”

He sat beside her. Across the garden, Gordon was explaining something to a robin, which listened from the handle of a fork.

“Have you put anything in?” Vera asked.

“Not yet.”

“Me neither.”

They drank their coffee.

After a while, Martin took a pencil from his pocket. He always carried one, although he no longer needed to. Vera handed him the blank back of a receipt.

He rested it on his knee.

There were things he might have written about work, or June, or the strange difficulty of a Tuesday with no obligations. He thought of the person who had got the job, or had hoped to. He thought of the child making a modest request of the future.

Finally, he wrote:

**The repaired slat is the second from the left. It should last a good while.**

Vera read it.

“Very you.”

“Too dull?”

“No.”

He folded the paper and put it in the box.

Then he sat down again, leaving room beside him.
